Princess the Unicorn

Come along with me — through the Rainbow Forest, magic wild and free!

Story Bible, assembled 2026-09-04 from the universe files SCRPT reads (profile.json, plates, poses, atlas, objects, scripts). Register: magical wonder — Disney-family warmth, nothing scary.

World rules

  1. RAINBOW FOREST HAS ONE CAVE: the spring cave behind the crack at the foot of the white cliff at Moonwater Spring, seen only in the scenes set there. Everywhere else, cliffs, banks and hillsides are solid unbroken pale rock with moss and flowers.
  2. THE GROUND is soft grass, bare earth path and small flat pebbles. Objects the story names appear exactly where the shot says and nowhere else.
  3. EVERY CHARACTER'S THINGS are on the character: a bell hangs at the neck of whoever wears it and appears only there.
  4. SOUND CUES name concrete things — water over stones, hoofsteps, leaves, small birds, a bell. Never wind, breeze, whisper, murmur, hum, sigh, echo or 'distant': a sound generator turns those into a voice.
  5. Fireflies are tiny soft yellow-green points of light — plain glowing dots with no bodies, wings or faces; they are never drawn as insects or little characters.

Size chart

SIZE CHART — obey exactly, in every shot of every episode. Glitter is a full-grown unicorn mare. Princess is a small foal: her back reaches only to Glitter's knee, and she is about one third of Glitter's length. Moss the little dragon is SMALLER than Princess — standing, his head reaches Princess's chest. Pip the bird is tiny: about the size of Princess's head, and he can perch on her back. These sizes NEVER change.

Episode format

Princess the Unicorn — Episode Format (v2, 12-minute)

The strict format every episode follows. v2 (Lars, 2026-08-30) folds in the Daniel Tiger analysis (research/daniel-tiger-structure.md): one strategy song per episode, the repetition ladder, learner-becomes- teacher, and direct address — inside our own fairy-tale register. This document is LAW for the storyboard, the storytelling and the dialogue: the board builder injects the FORMAT RULES section verbatim into its prompts; the fixed bookends are attached mechanically by the pipeline. The goal: 100 episodes, each one only as much new work as its story.

The house six beats (see universe/EPISODE-STRUCTURE.md)

1. Intro — theme song · 2. Episode introduction — wide world image, storyteller sets up today, move in to the characters (instrumental) · 3. The main chunk — pictures, dialogue, storyteller throughout · 4. The episode ending — storyteller sums up, PRINCESS says what we learned today, storyteller closes (at dusk, never in bed) · 5. THE END — the lullaby scene, the only bedtime · 6. Credits — TigerWorks · France 2026 over a short instrumental of the theme.

The fixed skeleton (~12:00)

| # | Beat | Length | Source |

|---|------|--------|--------|

| 1 | Show intro — sung theme, logo hop + blink | ~0:20 | `show-intro-v8.mp4`, identical every episode |
| 2 | Valley opening — widest view of Rainbow Forest, camera drifts in; theme continuation enters inside the intro's white fade | ~0:10 | per episode |
| 3 | Storyteller + hello — Sarah sets the morning ("Every morning in Rainbow Forest…"), teases today's story; Princess greets the viewer directly ("Hi, friend!") before any dialogue between characters | ~0:40 | per episode |
| 4 | The ordinary morning — motifs live here (the bell, the sparkle); the day's want appears | ~1:00 | per episode |
| 5 | Travel ritual — the gallop/rainbow-path transition with its own short sung line, same melody every episode | ~0:15 | recurring asset once minted |
| 6 | The wobble — the day's small problem arises; feelings named in plain words | ~1:00 | per episode |
| 7 | STRATEGY SONG introduced — the episode's adult sings the strategy line at the first moment of need | ~0:30 | per episode (one new song line per episode) |
| 8 | The repetition ladder — the line returns in 3 new situations; midway, one make-believe/wonder interlude (~0:45) for pure visual magic | ~5:00 | per episode |
| 9 | Learner becomes teacher — Princess uses the strategy for someone ELSE; the lesson is named once, plainly | ~1:00 | per episode |
| 10 | Full recap verse — a longer sung pass of the strategy over quick vignettes of the day | ~1:00 | per episode (same melody as beat 7) |
| 11 | Home at dusk + direct address — the day settles; Princess (or the storyteller) hands the lesson to the viewer: "When YOU…?" | ~0:30 | per episode |
| 12 | Bedtime ending — Glitter tucks Princess in and sings The Unicorn Lullaby (short); asleep on the last note. THE only bedtime in the episode | ~0:26 | rotating set of lullaby animations (to be made) |
| 13 | Credits — TigerWorks card holds while the MAIN THEME plays as an instrumental, fading out | ~0:17 | `endcard-with-theme.mp4` (inside episode-outro) |

Music slots: sung theme → instrumental continuation → travel ritual line → strategy song (intro, ladder reprises, recap verse) → mood score → The Unicorn Lullaby. The lullaby is ALWAYS the ending. Every episode mints one new strategy song — they feed the streaming/bedtime-album verticals.

FORMAT RULES (injected into the board builder's prompts)

RULES OF THE SERIES — every episode of Princess the Unicorn obeys these:

S1. THE SHAPE OF A DAY: every episode is one day in Rainbow Forest — it begins in the morning ("Every morning in Rainbow Forest…" is the storyteller's home key) and settles toward EVENING. The story itself ends at dusk — homecoming, celebration, calm — but NEVER in bed: bedtime happens exactly once per episode, in the standard lullaby outro that follows (Lars, 2026-08-30: the story showed Princess going to bed twice in a row). Write toward dusk, not toward sleep. S2. THE STORYTELLER opens (world first, then the tease of today's story, concrete and story-true), and PRINCESS GREETS THE VIEWER directly ("Hi, friend!") before any character-to-character dialogue. The storyteller may return for one short bridge and one warm closing line; the characters carry everything else. S3. ONE ADVENTURE, ONE LESSON, ONE SONG: each episode has exactly one small adventure and one gentle lesson a 3–6-year-old can SING — the lesson is written as a single melodic STRATEGY LINE (8–12 words, e.g. "When you can't hear the bell, stop and listen well"). A warm adult (usually Glitter) sings it at the first moment of need — never a lecture before the need exists. S4. THE REPETITION LADDER: after its introduction the strategy line returns at least three times, each in a NEW situation, sung or spoken — and it must GENERALIZE: first Princess needs it, then someone else does. Near the end comes a fuller RECAP VERSE: the same melody sung over quick vignettes of the day's moments. S5. LEARNER BECOMES TEACHER: the emotional high point is Princess using the strategy on someone else's behalf — she teaches what she just learned. Mastery is shown, never announced. S6. THE ARC: ordinary morning → the wobble (a small thing goes wrong or a wonder appears) → strategy introduced → the ladder (three tries or three steps — kids count in threes; the FIRST try may fail — plan B calmly) → Princess teaches it → home, calmer than we left → bedtime. If someone caused the wobble, they help mend it and are thanked, never shamed — a mistake is met with kindness and a job to do. S7. STAKES stay small and warm: no villains, no danger of harm — only mishaps, weather, distances, waiting and misunderstandings. The disruption is EMOTIONAL (worry, impatience, missing someone) and the feeling is named in plain words ("I miss Mama"). S8. DIALOGUE for small ears: short lines (a breath each), concrete words, warm use of names. Once per episode a character may ask the VIEWER something and pause a beat ("Can YOU see the bell?"). S9. THE MOTIFS repeat every episode: Glitter's silver bell (safety and home), Princess's "Ring, ring, ring!" delight, the sparkle that marks magic, the travel ritual's sung line. One motif at the start, one at the resolution. S10. ONE MAKE-BELIEVE INTERLUDE mid-episode (~45s): a wonder sequence riffing on the theme — pure visual magic, no plot advancement, then back to the story. S11. THE CAST is the cast: Princess, Glitter, Pip, Moss, the Fireflies. A visitor may pass through for one episode; the family solves the day. Never a new main character. S12. EVERY SHOT obeys the house camera rules: the first story shot is the widest view of the valley drifting in (no character close in shot 1); faces visible, front or three-quarter; painted storybook style, never photoreal. S13. THE ENDING HANDS IT OVER: before bed, Princess (or the storyteller) asks the viewer the lesson's question directly ("When YOU can't hear your mama, what do you do?") — then the lullaby. S14. BEDTIME IS SACRED: the last story beat settles everything. No cliffhangers, no open questions — the day is complete, Princess is safe, the forest holds her near.

THE STORYTELLER'S VOICE (how every narration line is written — full craft book: storyteller-voice.md): V1. She has FIVE slots only: the OPENING ("Every morning in Rainbow Forest began the same sweet way." + one sensory line + who we find, three sentences max), the TEASE ("But today would be different. Today, Princess would [concrete adventure] — and learn [lesson in a four-year-old's words]."), at most ONE two-sentence BRIDGE at the wobble that names the feeling plainly, the HANDOVER (one direct question to the child near the end, then a beat of silence), and the GOODNIGHT ("And as the stars came out over Rainbow Forest…"), whose last word lands on safe/warm/home/near. V2. Concrete words only (sun, bell, fog, blanket); "brave" yes, "courage" no. Short sentences, one breath each; fourteen words is long. Repetition is warmth — she reuses the episode's own words. V3. She adds FEELING to the picture, never description of what we can already see. She loves the characters out loud ("our little unicorn"). Never scary, never ironic, never during dialogue. V4. IN A FILM she is a continuous thread (Lars, 2026-08-30: the voiceover does the storytelling): besides her five slots she marks EVERY scene transition a child could lose — how the hero got here, why they go there next, any change of place or point of view — eight to ten touches in a 10-12 minute film. If a viewer closed their eyes, her words alone should still carry the story.

Production notes (for the pipeline, not the prompts)

- Target length: 12 minutes (board at minutes=12). Boards tend to come back short (episode one planned ~6.5 min of picture → ~10 min cut; accepted by Lars 2026-08-30, episode one only). FROM EPISODE TWO: if a board's estimated seconds land under ~80% of target, extend the repetition ladder with one more situation AND the wonder interlude before accepting the board. - Storyteller voice: profile voice_cast.Storyteller (Sarah). Character voices: profile voice_cast; book-level overrides win. - Strategy songs: sung by the cast's voices; each episode's line + recap verse are minted per episode and archived in the profile (strategy_songs) — they compound into albums. - Faces: cast plates + drawn board frame travel with EVERY shot. No frame, no shoot. - Bookends attach mechanically from the profile (show_intro, show_outro / lullaby_endings rotation once the variants exist). - Episode pairing (series craft): teach a strategy in one episode, generalize it in a sibling episode later in the season. - YouTube unit = BOTH: single episodes AND stitched compilations (~40–90 min, the watch-time format — Lars 2026-08-30, confirmed by Rainbow Ruby/Daniel Tiger channels). In a compilation only the first episode carries the show intro and only the last the end card; episodes chain lullaby → next valley opening, seamlessly. Per-episode rituals still repeat — rituals are retention; repeated intros are churn. - Storyteller craft book: storyteller-voice.md. - Reference analyses: research/daniel-tiger-structure.md, research/rainbow-ruby-structure.md.

The Storyteller's Book

The Storyteller's Book — Princess the Unicorn

How the voiceover speaks. The storyteller (Sarah) is a grandmother telling a bedtime story she loves: warm, unhurried, always smiling, speaking TO the child — never over them. She is the frame of every episode; the characters are the picture. The compact V-rules live in episode-format.md and are injected into every board build; this book is the full craft reference with examples.

Her five slots — and ONLY these five

1. THE OPENING (fixed home key). Every episode begins:

"Every morning in Rainbow Forest began the same sweet way."

Then ONE sensory line of the morning — things a child can see or hear (sun, birdsong, dew, the bell) — then who we find and what they are doing. Three sentences, never more.

*"Every morning in Rainbow Forest began the same sweet way. The birds
were singing, the sun was shining, and Princess and her mama Glitter
were out on their morning walk."*

2. THE TEASE (fixed pivot). Always the "But today…" turn — concrete and story-true, adventure first, lesson last, lesson in words a four-year-old says:

*"But today would be different. Today, Princess would chase a tiny cry
into the fog, meet two brand-new friends — and learn what to do when
you can't hear your mama's bell."*

3. THE BRIDGE (at most one per episode). A soft turn or a time-skip at the wobble — two sentences maximum, and it NAMES THE FEELING plainly:

*"The fog was everywhere now. And for the very first time, Princess
felt small, and lost, and far from home."*

4. THE HANDOVER (near the end). One direct question to the child, then a beat of silence before anyone speaks:

"When YOU can't find your mama — what do you do?"

5. THE GOODNIGHT (fixed home key). Over the dusk scene, leading into the lullaby:

*"And as the stars came out over Rainbow Forest, Princess snuggled
deep into her moss bed — safe, and warm, and home."*

The last word of the episode's narration always lands on safe / warm / home / near.

Her language

- Concrete words only: sun, bell, fog, blanket, hooves. "Brave" yes; "courage" no; "resilience" never. - Short sentences — one breath each, spoken slowly (the 0.88 pace). Fourteen words is a long sentence for her. - Repetition is warmth, not error: "the same sweet way… sweet dreams." She reuses the episode's own words when she returns. - She adds feeling to the picture, never description of it. If we can see the fog, she tells us how the fog FEELS. - She loves the characters out loud: "our little unicorn." - She never rushes plot — the characters do plot. She frames it. - She is never scary, never ironic, never clever at the child's expense. - She never speaks during a dialogue scene, and never appears more than six times in an episode (five slots + at most one extra bridge beat).

Why this shape

Daniel Tiger has no narrator — the hero addresses the child. Rainbow Ruby has none either. The storyteller is OUR signature: the fairy-tale frame neither reference has. But a frame only works if it is a ritual — the same voice, the same home keys, the same five doors in and out of the story, every single episode. A child should be able to say the opening and the goodnight along with her by episode three.

Episode structure

The TigerWorks Episode Structure

The house shape of every animated episode, in every universe (Lars, 2026-08-30). A universe may name its beats in its own language, but the six beats and their order never change.

The six beats

1. INTRO — the theme song. The universe's sung title sequence. Identical every episode; never re-made per story. Ends on its signature (Princess: the wink + bell pling).

2. EPISODE INTRODUCTION — instrumental music. One big wide image of the story world, the storyteller welcoming the audience and setting up today's story, then the camera moves in to the characters and the story begins. The instrumental continuation of the theme carries this and bows out as the first dialogue lands.

3. THE MAIN CHUNK — the story. Told through pictures, dialogue and a great deal of storytelling from the voiceover: the voiceover is a continuous thread, marking every turn a child could lose (see V-rules). One adventure, one lesson, the strategy song and its ladder, one wonder interlude.

4. THE EPISODE ENDING — the sum-up. Three movements, in order: (a) the storyteller sums up the story now that it is over; (b) THE CONCLUSION WISDOM — the main character says, in their own child-simple words, what we learned today; (c) the storyteller closes the main chunk warmly. The story ends at DUSK — homecoming, celebration, calm — never in bed.

5. THE END — the lullaby scene. The universe's fixed bedtime ending: the main character goes to bed and the lullaby is sung. This is the ONLY bedtime in the episode. Same song every episode, a small rotating set of animations.

6. CREDITS. The end card — "TigerWorks · France 2026", white on black, minimalist — while a short instrumental of the main theme plays and fades out.

Why it holds

Beats 1, 5 and 6 are fixed assets: made once per universe, attached mechanically, never re-made per episode. Beats 2, 3 and 4 are the only new work a story requires. That is what makes 26 — or 100 — episodes possible.

The first law of the script (Lars, 2026-08-31)

THE SCRIPT IS THE FILM. It is written to work with the eyes closed — a listener who never sees a picture must follow the whole story, feel every turn and understand the ending. It must stand on its own as an audiobook.

The pictures only underline and strengthen what the words already carry. They are never asked to explain anything: if a beat can only be understood by seeing it, the script is wrong.

This inverts the old order (board first, words fitted afterwards) and is why the pipeline now runs: script → approve → illustrate → shoot. Every spoken beat becomes exactly one shot carrying that beat alone — one voice at a time — and a shot's length is decided by its words (words / 2.2 + a beat to breathe), never the other way round.

THE LENGTH OF AN EPISODE — 8 MINUTES (Lars, 2026-08-31)

An episode is 8 minutes, finished, including both bookends:

intro (0:20) + story (≈7:04) + lullaby ending & credits (0:36)

That is a word budget, not a feeling. Measured on our own cast at speed 0.9, the voices read 2.68 words per second. A film also has to breathe — roughly a second of picture per beat with nobody talking. So:

spoken words ≈ (424s − beats × 1s) × 2.68 ≈ 800–870 words of speech, in about 70–80 beats

For comparison: script v5 ran 1,769 words and read 11:40 aloud — more than twice the budget. Write to the budget from the start; a script cut in half after it is written loses its shape.

Cut dialogue before you cut narration. The storyteller is what makes the story followable; character chatter is what makes it long. Keep the storyteller at 60–65% of the words.

HOW THE STORYTELLER SPEAKS TO A FOUR-YEAR-OLD (Lars, 2026-08-31)

These are not style preferences. A four-year-old loses the story at the first unnamed thing.

1. Name the thing. Never point at it. Not "that sound" — "the sound of Mama's bell". Not "there was no ring, ring, ring" — "there was no ringing, no sound of Mama's bell, in the whole forest". A child cannot follow a pronoun back three sentences. 2. Name the people. Never "they". Not "they were walking home" — "Princess and her mum were walking home". Every sentence says who. 3. One idea per sentence. Short sentences, concrete words, no subordinate clauses stacked on each other, no poetic inversions. If a sentence needs a comma to hold two thoughts, it is two sentences. 4. The storyteller tells the story; the characters live in it. Narration carries every place, every plan and every cause — 60–65% of the words. This was the single biggest improvement between v4 and v5.

LENGTH — about 12 minutes (Lars, 2026-08-31, after hearing v5 read)

The 8-minute target set earlier the same day is withdrawn. Heard as audio, script v5 ran 11:40 and Lars judged it right: "We need that time to properly tell the story." Write for the story, not for a clock — an episode lands between 10 and 12 minutes. Our cast reads 2.68 words per second, so that is roughly 1,600–1,900 spoken words.

EVERY LINE CARRIES ITS DIRECTION (Lars, 2026-08-31)

Recording runs on eleven_v3, which acts an inline note the way a screenplay carries a parenthetical: [frightened] Mama? The old models do not act it — they READ IT ALOUD. That was heard on the control test: Princess said the word "frightened" instead of sounding it. The recorder therefore attaches a direction only on a model that can act it and strips every bracket on any other model, so a wrong model degrades to a flat read and never to nonsense.

Each character has a standing direction in the universe profile; a line may override it with its own direction. The storyteller's standing direction is warm, gentle, caring, unhurried — never dramatic, and that holds hardest on the saddest line in the film.

THE SHOT GRAMMAR OF CHILDREN'S ANIMATION (Lars, 2026-08-31)

A small child must always be able to tell who is there and what is happening. Adult television grammar hides both.

Always: eye level, at the child's height. Camera steady. Characters whole in frame — full figure or medium — side by side with air between them, both faces visible when they speak to each other. A close-up is a single face, straight on, holding one feeling.

Never: over-the-shoulder shots, framing past a body or through foreground objects, tilted angles, extreme high or low angles, handheld, whip pans, orbits, rack focus, or any framing that crops a face or cuts a character in half.

Camera moves are slow and simple: a gentle push in, a slow drift, or nothing at all.

Mouths. Voices are recorded separately, so a tight close-up on a talking mouth never matches. Frame the character who is SPEAKING full figure or medium, and save the close-up for the one who is listening, deciding, or feeling something.

Season format

HOW A SEASON WORKS — the house format

Applies to every children's universe. A season is not a pile of episodes; it is a block that can be produced, released and watched as a unit — while every single episode still stands completely on its own.

The two rules that must both hold

1. Any episode is a child's first episode. No episode may require another. The rule is re-taught inside the story every time. A returning friend introduces themself in one line ("I'm Moss — I'm afraid of nearly everything"). The finale explains its own stakes from scratch.

2. A season rewards the child who stays. Continuity is carried by things a returning viewer notices and a new viewer never misses: a growing cast, a changing world, and a collection.

The four things that make a season a season

The season question. One developmental theme, asked twelve to twenty-four times in different clothes. Season one of Princess is "Can I manage what I feel?" — every episode is a feeling met and survived.

The growing cast. Two or three new friends per season. Each gets one episode where they arrive and are properly introduced; afterwards they appear in the background of other episodes without explanation. A child who has watched them all sees a fuller forest; a child watching one sees a full forest anyway.

The turning year. A season sits in one stretch of the year. Season one runs spring into summer; season two runs autumn into winter and out the other side. Children mark time by weather, and it gives the films visual variety without changing the world.

The collection. Something visible accumulates. Princess earns her own silver bell in episode one; from then on each adventure adds one small charm to the ribbon. By the finale the bell carries twelve — a record of the season a child can see and count, that never once needs explaining.

The shape of a season

| Episode | Job |

|---|---|

| 1 | The **origin** of the season's question, and the strongest single story. It must work as the only episode anyone ever sees. |
| 2–4 | The question in easy clothes. Small, warm, funny. Establish the rhythm. |
| 5 | **New friend one** arrives. |
| 6–8 | Harder feelings. The first episode where the lesson costs something. |
| 9 | **New friend two** arrives. |
| 10–11 | The learner becomes the teacher: Princess helps somebody else use the rule. |
| 12 | **The finale**: the season's question at its widest, every recurring friend on screen, and the collection complete. Still standalone. |

Longer seasons (18 or 24) repeat the 5/9 arrival beat and the learner-becomes-teacher pair, and add one special: a double-length episode at the turn of the year.

Release

Singles weekly. Every three episodes, a compilation (~33 minutes) — that is where the watch time lives. At season end, the full-season compilation and the season's book box. Books release in episode order; the audiobook of each is the film's own soundtrack.

Stories

Episode 1 — Princess and the Hidden Spring (shooting manuscript v8)

PRINCESS AND THE HIDDEN SPRING

Episode 1 — SHOOTING MANUSCRIPT v8 (ten minutes)

Trimmed from v7 against episode1-story-chain.json: all 22 load-bearing links and all 6 setup–payoff pairs intact. What left was repetition, banter, and lines where a character said something the storyteller had already said.

Voices — STORYTELLER David (warm, gentle, caring — never dramatic) · PRINCESS Tilly · GLITTER Beth · PIP Aurelia · MOSS Valf · FIREFLIES Emily. Every line carries its direction. Recording on eleven_v3.

1 · A MORNING IN RAINBOW FOREST

STORYTELLER (warm, gentle): Far away, where the rainbows go to rest, there is a forest. It is called Rainbow Forest. And every morning in Rainbow Forest begins with the same happy sound.

The sound of a silver bell. Ring, ring, ring.

STORYTELLER (warm, smiling): That is the sound of a little silver bell. The bell belongs to a big, kind unicorn called Glitter. And the little unicorn walking next to her is her daughter. Her name is Princess.

PRINCESS (bright, friendly, to the audience): Good morning, friend! My mum and I are going for our morning walk. Will you come?

2 · MAMA'S RULE

STORYTELLER (warm): Princess and her mum walked in under the big flowers, where the morning mist lies soft on the path.

GLITTER (warm, tender): Stay close enough to hear my bell, little one.

PRINCESS (happy): I can always hear your bell, Mama.

GLITTER (gentle, teaching): And if one day you cannot hear it — do you remember our rule?

PRINCESS (proud, careful): Stop. Listen. And go to Moonwater Spring.

GLITTER (warm, certain): That is right. Moonwater Spring is our meeting place. And I will always come there to find you.

STORYTELLER (warm, kind): Remember Mama's rule, friend. Princess is going to need it today.

3 · MOONWATER SPRING

STORYTELLER (warm, wondering): The meeting place is a little pool of water in a green clearing, and it shines like the moon, even in the morning. That is why it is called Moonwater Spring.

PRINCESS (delighted): Mmm! This water tastes like starlight.

STORYTELLER (warm): The water from Moonwater Spring runs away under the ground. It gives a drink to every flower and every tree in Rainbow Forest.

PRINCESS (curious): Does the whole forest drink this water, Mama?

GLITTER (warm, simple): Every drop, my love.

STORYTELLER (gentle, quietly marking it): High above the pool stands a white cliff. Look at the big white stones on top of it, friend. Those big white stones have been waiting up there for a very, very long time. And today, they are going to fall.

4 · THE STONES COME DOWN

STORYTELLER (warm, calm): Princess and her mum walked back along the path towards home. Then the forest made a sound.

A long, low rumble.

PRINCESS (a little worried): Mama? What is that noise?

GLITTER (calm, reassuring): It is only the old stones on the cliff, my love.

STORYTELLER (gentle, clear): But it was more than that. Up on the cliff, the white stones came sliding down, and grey dust flew up into the trees.

STORYTELLER (gentle, clear): And one round white stone rolled into the little hole where the water comes out, and stuck fast. Now the water could not get out at all. Nobody saw that stone, friend. Only you and me.

5 · THE LITTLE LIGHTS

FIREFLIES (tiny, frightened): Help! Somebody help us, please!

PRINCESS (alert, kind): Mama, wait! Somebody is calling for help!

STORYTELLER (warm): The shaking had knocked a branch out of a tree, and it had trapped a family of fireflies in the vines.

PRINCESS (gentle, brave): Don't be frightened, little lights. I will get you out.

STORYTELLER (warm, careful): So Princess stayed. She lifted the branch with her horn, very carefully, until every firefly wriggled out.

FIREFLIES (bright, happy): We are free! Thank you, Princess!

STORYTELLER (gentle, this is the turn): But while Princess was helping the fireflies, her mum kept walking. Glitter was calling Princess's name, and ringing her silver bell. But the dust was thick between them, and Princess did not hear her mum at all.

PRINCESS (happy, then uncertain): I did it, Mama! Mama? Where are you?

STORYTELLER (gentle, sad but warm): And the path in front of Princess was empty. She was a long way from home.

6 · STOP. LISTEN. GO.

PRINCESS (calling, worried): Mama! Mama, where are you?

STORYTELLER (gentle): Princess started to run. Then Princess stopped herself, and remembered the first part of Mama's rule.

PRINCESS (steadying herself): Stop. Listen.

STORYTELLER (gentle, quiet): So Princess stood very still, and she listened as hard as she could.

PRINCESS (hopeful, then small): Can you hear Mama's bell, friend? No. I cannot hear it either.

STORYTELLER (gentle, tender): There was no ringing anywhere. There was no sound of Mama's bell in the whole forest. And for somebody very small, that is a very big feeling.

PRINCESS (frightened, small, trembling): I think I am lost.

PRINCESS (deciding, brave): But I know our rule. Go to Moonwater Spring. Mama will come there. I am going to walk there.

STORYTELLER (warm, clear): And now Princess had a plan. She was very small, and she was not sure of the way. But she knew where she was going.

7 · PIP THE BIRD

PIP (quick, cheerful, curious): Chirp! Hello! Who are you calling for?

STORYTELLER (warm): A little blue bird hopped out of the dust. The bird was called Pip.

PRINCESS (polite, hopeful): My mum. She will be at Moonwater Spring. But I don't know the way from here.

PIP (bright, proud): Then it is lucky you met me! Moonwater Spring is that way, over the rope bridge.

STORYTELLER (warm, kind): And that was the second good thing Princess did today. When Princess could not do it on her own, Princess asked for help.

8 · MOSS THE LITTLE DRAGON

STORYTELLER (warm): The way to the spring goes over a rope bridge, high above a river.

MOSS (nervous, shaky, small): Please don't step on my tail!

STORYTELLER (warm): Out from under the bridge came a little green dragon, shaking from his nose to the end of his tail. His name was Moss.

MOSS (nervous, small): I want to cross. But I am afraid of high places.

PRINCESS (warm, inviting): Come with us, Moss. We are going to Moonwater Spring.

MOSS (worried): But I am not brave.

PRINCESS (kind, certain): Being brave does not mean you are not scared, Moss. It means you keep going, even when you are.

STORYTELLER (warm): And Princess and Pip and Moss crossed the rope bridge together. Step by step, slowly and carefully.

9 · THE SPRING HAS GONE DARK

STORYTELLER (gentle, concerned): But when the three friends came into the green clearing, Princess stopped very suddenly.

PRINCESS (shocked, quiet): Look at the spring. The water has gone.

STORYTELLER (gentle): Moonwater Spring was not shining any more. There were only wet grey stones, and one thin little trickle of water.

PRINCESS (working it out, then certain): Look up at the cliff. The white stones have fallen down. That was the rumble I heard this morning. Now the water cannot get out.

STORYTELLER (warm, proud of her): And Princess was right. The three friends followed the little trickle to a crack in the cliff, and a dark, quiet cave.

PRINCESS (worried, clear): The whole forest drinks this water. But I am not going into a dark cave without a light.

10 · THE LITTLE LIGHTS COME BACK

PRINCESS (calling, hopeful): Little lights! Fireflies! We need your help!

STORYTELLER (warm, delighted): And out from the trees came the fireflies Princess had helped that morning. They flew into the crack in the cliff, and their little lights made a golden path into the dark.

MOSS (small, honest): I am still afraid, Princess.

PRINCESS (warm, honest): So am I, Moss. We can be afraid and brave at the same time.

11 · ONE BRAVE FLAP AT A TIME

STORYTELLER (gentle, clear): Deep inside the cave, one big round white stone was stuck in the mouth of an underground river. The water pushed and pushed behind it, and could not get past.

PRINCESS (recognising it): That is the stone that fell this morning. We have to move it. Push!

STORYTELLER (warm): Princess pushed as hard as she could. The stone did not move.

PIP (bright, rallying): It is not too heavy for all three of us! I will pull from the side.

PRINCESS (planning): Moss, we need somebody on top of the stone.

MOSS (afraid): But I cannot fly.

PRINCESS (warm, believing in him): You crossed the bridge, Moss. And you were afraid. Just one brave flap at a time.

STORYTELLER (warm, rising): And Moss flapped his wings once. And twice. And up went Moss!

MOSS (amazed, joyful): I am flying! I am really flying!

PRINCESS (strong, leading): Ready? One. Two. Three. Push!

STORYTELLER (warm, joyful): And the big white stone rolled away. And the water came rushing out, bright and shining, out of the cave and into the forest.

12 · TWO SILVER BELLS

STORYTELLER (warm, happy): Out in the clearing, Moonwater Spring filled up and began to shine again. And then Princess heard a sound.

Ring, ring, ring.

PRINCESS (overjoyed): Mama! That is Mama's bell!

GLITTER (calling, full of love): Princess!

GLITTER (tender, holding her): Oh, my brave girl. I have been walking to this spring since the morning.

PRINCESS (happy, understanding): You came to our meeting place.

GLITTER (warm, certain): Of course I did. That is our rule. I knew that if I waited here, you would come.

PRINCESS (proud, telling it): I stopped, Mama. And I listened. And then I walked here. And Pip and Moss helped me.

MOSS (proud, still amazed): And I flew!

STORYTELLER (warm, tender): And Glitter lifted a little silver bell out from under her mane, just the right size for Princess.

GLITTER (tender): Now you know exactly what to do when you cannot hear me.

PRINCESS (delighted): Ring, ring, ring! It sounds just like your bell, Mama!

13 · WHAT WE LEARNED TODAY

This scene, and only this scene, is shown in the storybook look: illustrated pages with a soft painted border.

STORYTELLER (warm, gentle): And that was the day the white stones came down in Rainbow Forest, and Princess found her own way to the meeting place.

PRINCESS (warm, to the audience): Friend? I learned something today. If you cannot find somebody you love, do not run. Stop. Listen. And go to the place you both know. That is where they will be looking for you.

PRINCESS (warm, simple): And if the way is too big for you, ask a friend to help. Pip and Moss helped me.

STORYTELLER (warm, gentle, closing): The evening came down soft and gold over Rainbow Forest. And on the path home, two silver bells were ringing together. One big bell, and one little bell.

THE END — the lullaby

Fixed bookend: Glitter tucks Princess into her moss bed and sings the Unicorn Lullaby. Princess falls asleep on the last note.

CREDITS

Fixed bookend: the two credit screens over the theme. Ten seconds.

Short 1 — Princess and the Lost Bell

PRINCESS AND THE LOST BELL

Short film 1 — SHOOTING MANUSCRIPT v1 (three and a half minutes)

A stand-alone short in the Princess the Unicorn universe: same cast, same world, one small story. Built on the extended foundation (Lars, 2026-09-03): pose sheets for every character, wide atlas plates for every place, one approved image per object STATE. House rules: no clip longer than five seconds, no lip sync — voices act over closed mouths.

Voices — STORYTELLER David (warm, gentle, caring — never dramatic) · PRINCESS Tilly · GLITTER Beth · PIP Aurelia · MOSS Valf.

Object set — glitter-bell (states: on-the-ribbon / lying-in-grass / in-a-foal-mouth) · hollow-log (states: empty / moss-peeking-out).

Places (atlas) — valley-from-above · meadow-by-the-river · hollow-log-clearing · path-home-dusk-wide.

1 · THE VALLEY

[place: valley-from-above]

STORYTELLER (warm, gentle): Far away, where the rainbows go to rest, there is a valley.

STORYTELLER (warm): In the valley lives a small unicorn called Princess, and her mother, Glitter.

STORYTELLER (warm, smiling): Around Glitter's neck hangs a small silver bell. When Princess hears it, she knows her mother is near.

The sound of the silver bell. Ring, ring.

2 · THE QUIET MEADOW

[place: meadow-by-the-river]

STORYTELLER (soft): One morning the meadow was very quiet.

PRINCESS (small, calling): Mama?

STORYTELLER (soft): No bell. Only the river, and the wind in the grass.

STORYTELLER (warm): Princess looked in the tall grass. She looked by the river. She looked under the big leaves.

PRINCESS (worried): I can't hear the bell.

3 · PIP

[place: meadow-by-the-river]

STORYTELLER (brightening): Then a small blue bird landed on a stone in front of her. It was Pip.

PIP (cheerful, kind): Why the long face, Princess?

PRINCESS (sad): Mama's bell is gone. Without the bell, I can't find her.

PIP (cheerful, certain): Then we will look with four eyes instead of two.

STORYTELLER (warm): Pip flew high and looked down. Princess walked low and looked under things.

4 · THE HOLLOW LOG

[place: hollow-log-clearing]

STORYTELLER (warm, wondering): By the old hollow log, something shone in the grass.

PIP (excited): There! Something silver!

STORYTELLER (warm): It was the bell. Its ribbon had come loose, and it had rolled into the grass.

STORYTELLER (gentle): But the bell had rolled far under the log, and Princess was too big to crawl in.

STORYTELLER (warm, amused): Out from the hollow log came a little green dragon, shaking from his nose to the end of his tail.

MOSS (frightened, small): Is it a snake? I am afraid of snakes.

PRINCESS (kind, gentle): It is not a snake, Moss. It is my mama's bell.

MOSS (relieved, brave): Oh. Then I can help. I am not afraid of bells.

STORYTELLER (warm): Moss reached in with his long tail and pushed the bell along the grass, all the way to Princess.

5 · TING

[place: hollow-log-clearing]

STORYTELLER (warm): Princess picked up the ribbon in her teeth. The bell went ting.

The bell. One clear ring.

STORYTELLER (warm, hopeful): And far across the meadow, someone heard it.

STORYTELLER (bright): Glitter came running.

GLITTER (relieved, tender): Princess! I have been looking everywhere for you.

PRINCESS (happy, a little proud): And I have been looking everywhere for you. Your bell fell off.

STORYTELLER (warm): Glitter bent her head, and Princess hung the bell back on its ribbon.

GLITTER (warm, certain): Now we will never lose each other.

6 · HOME

[place: path-home-dusk-wide]

STORYTELLER (warm, gentle): That evening, three friends walked home together along the golden path.

STORYTELLER (warm, smiling): And every step of the way, the little bell went ting, ting, ting.

The bell, three soft rings, fading.

STORYTELLER (soft): The end.
